Yes, the story has an appropriate and effective balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The author uses exposition and summary at the beginning and end of the story—as well as at the start of each section—to compress time, establish the narrator's family dynamics, and convey the broader context of her father's illness and eventual passing. This groundwork gives emotional weight to the dramatized scenes that form the heart of the narrative, such as the brief conversation with Marcus by the pool, the quiet confession with Eli at the ship's rail, and the climactic dance with her father at the White Party. By alternating seamlessly between compressed reflection and real-time interaction, the story maintains a steady, engaging pace and builds deep emotional resonance without feeling rushed or bogged down.
